beats: Alright, Kaustubh, let’s pause a moment and think about why databases can handle so many users at once without stepping on each other’s toes. The trick is that every piece of data gets a little “guard” – a lock – that tells a transaction whether it can read or write that item right now. By coordinating those locks correctly we prevent nasty anomalies like lost updates or inconsistent reads, and we keep the whole system behaving as if the transactions were running one after another. So, understanding how these locks work is the foundation for any solid concurrency‑control strategy.

Alright, Kaustubh, picture the lock as a little sign that hangs on each row or page of the table – it can be “free”, “shared” or “exclusive”. When a transaction just wants to look at the data it asks for a shared lock; the lock manager bumps the counter up and lets any number of other readers join in, but as soon as someone needs to change the value it must first grab an exclusive lock, which forces everyone else to wait until the lock is released. The lock manager does this with three primitive calls – `read_lock(x)`, `write_lock(x)` and `unlock(x)` – and it keeps a small table that records which transaction holds which lock and how many readers are currently attached. Now, the trick that makes everything safe is the two‑phase rule: during the “growing” phase a transaction can keep asking for more locks, but once it releases its first lock it enters the “shrinking” phase and is no longer allowed to acquire any new ones. If a transaction that started with a shared lock later decides it needs to write, it can try to upgrade to an exclusive lock; the upgrade succeeds only if it’s the sole reader at that moment, otherwise it has to wait – that’s the lock‑conversion nuance. Let’s walk through a concrete scenario: suppose T1 does `read_lock(A)`, reads the balance, then `read_lock(B)` and reads a second account; meanwhile T2 asks for `write_lock(A)` to transfer money out of that same account. Because T1 still holds a shared lock on A, T2 must wait; once T1 finishes its reads it calls `unlock(A)`, the lock manager notices there are no more readers, flips A to “unlocked”, and immediately grants the pending exclusive lock to T2, which can now safely update the balance. Only after T2 writes and calls `unlock(A)` does the lock become free again, allowing any other transaction to proceed – and because each transaction obeyed the grow‑then‑shrink pattern, we’ve avoided lost updates, dirty reads, and even deadlocks.

So, when you see those lock‑states and the two‑phase rule, think of them as the scaffolding that lets higher‑level techniques—like strict 2PL, conservative 2PL, or even lock‑free timestamp ordering—stand up without collapsing into anomalies or deadlocks. That’s why we spend time mastering the basics now: every advanced concurrency protocol builds on the same lock‑acquire, lock‑release discipline, and the way we enforce the grow‑then‑shrink pattern determines whether a schedule will be serializable, recoverable, or safe from cascading rollbacks. In the next part we’ll layer those variations on top, so you’ll see how a small tweak—say, holding all exclusive locks until commit—gives us strict 2PL and eliminates many of the pitfalls we just avoided. Got it, Kaustubh—can you tell me why a transaction must finish its growing phase before it starts releasing locks?

Think of it as a disciplined dance where a transaction first gathers all the locks it needs—its “growing” phase—before it ever lets any of them go, and then, once it starts releasing, it can’t pick up any new ones in the “shrinking” phase. This strict ordering is what guarantees that the interleaving of transactions will behave just like some serial order, so we don’t end up with weird, non‑serializable results. Later we’ll see a few twists on the basic idea—strict 2PL, conservative 2PL, and even multiversion variants—that each try to balance safety with more concurrency. Let’s dive in and see why getting this right is essential for a reliable database.

Alright, Kaustubh, let’s dig into how 2PL actually works under the hood. When a transaction starts, it keeps a table—think of it as a little ledger—that records every lock it holds on each data item, whether it’s a shared (read) lock or an exclusive (write) lock. During the **growing phase** the transaction may ask for new locks any time it needs to read or write, and the lock manager will either grant them immediately if they don’t conflict, or make the transaction wait until the conflicting lock is released. The moment the transaction decides to release its first lock, it enters the **shrinking phase**, and from that point on it’s forbidden to request any additional locks; it can only give up the ones it already has. If a transaction needs to upgrade a lock—say it first took a shared lock on X because it only read it, but later decides to write X—it can request an upgrade, but the upgrade must happen while still in the growing phase; otherwise the protocol would be broken. Conversely, a downgrade—from exclusive back to shared—is allowed only in the shrinking phase, after all the new lock requests have stopped. To see why this matters, picture two transactions T1 and T2: T1 reads X, then upgrades to a write lock on X, reads Y, and finally releases Y before releasing X; T2 meanwhile wants a read lock on Y, then a write lock on X. Because T1 releases Y first, T2 can acquire its read lock on Y, but when it later asks for the write lock on X it has to wait until T1 finally unlocks X—so the schedule respects the two‑phase rule and ends up equivalent to the serial order T1 → T2. If either transaction tried to grab a new lock after it had already started unlocking, the protocol would be violated and you could get a non‑serializable outcome like the one where X and Y both end up at 50. That’s the core idea: by enforcing a clean “grow‑then‑shrink” pattern, 2PL guarantees conflict‑serializability without having to examine the whole schedule afterward.

The idea is simple: every transaction gets a unique timestamp when it starts, and we use those timestamps to decide which reads and writes are allowed to proceed. By enforcing that operations happen in timestamp order, we can guarantee a serializable schedule without ever having to wait for a lock, which means we avoid deadlocks altogether. It matters because in high‑throughput systems the overhead of locking can become a bottleneck, and timestamp ordering gives us a clean, deterministic way to resolve conflicts. So think of timestamps as the invisible “time‑cards” that tell each transaction when it’s allowed to touch a data item.

That’s what Multiversion Concurrency Control does – it keeps multiple snapshots of data around so reads never have to wait for writes, and writes never have to block reads. The magic is that each transaction works with a committed version that’s safe for it, and only when it’s ready to commit does it replace the old version with a new one. This approach not only boosts parallelism, but also eliminates those nasty cascading aborts you saw with strict locking. In short, MVCC lets us have high‑throughput concurrent access while preserving the ACID guarantees we need.

Alright, Kaustubh, let me walk you through how MVCC actually works under the hood. When a transaction starts, it gets a snapshot timestamp and it only ever sees rows whose *commit* timestamp is older than that snapshot – those are the “old, committed versions.” If the transaction wants to update a row, it doesn’t overwrite the existing tuple; instead it writes a new version with its own commit‑time placeholder and marks the old one as superseded but still readable by anyone whose snapshot is earlier. When the transaction reaches the commit point it first grabs a *certify lock* on every row it has written – this lock guarantees that no other transaction is still reading the old version while we’re about to make the new version official. Once those certify locks are in place, the system flips the new version’s timestamp to the real commit time, discards the old version, and releases all the locks, so readers can now see the fresh data without ever having been blocked. Because readers never have to wait for writers, you get high parallelism, and because writers only ever read committed data, you avoid cascading aborts. Let’s see a concrete scenario: imagine T₁ starts at time 100 and reads a row R with commit‑time 80; meanwhile T₂ starts at time 110, updates R, and creates a new version with a provisional timestamp 110. T₁ continues its work oblivious to T₂’s change, because its snapshot is still at 100. When T₂ finally tries to commit, it acquires the certify lock on R, confirms that no transaction with a snapshot between 80 and 110 is still using the old version (T₁’s snapshot is 100, so it is), and then promotes its new version to commit‑time 120, discarding the old one. Now any transaction that starts after 120 will see the updated R, while T₁ already finished with the consistent view it saw at 100. That’s the essence of MVCC: versioned rows, snapshot timestamps, certify‑lock certification, and a clean hand‑off that keeps reads lock‑free and writes safe.

When your query finishes, that new “phantom” row shows up in the result set even though it wasn’t there when you started—so the data you read isn’t consistent. That’s the phantom phenomenon, and it can break the guarantees we rely on for correct concurrent execution. Understanding how to prevent those sneaky inserts—or deletes—within a query’s range is why we study phantom‑avoidance techniques now. It’s the missing piece that lets our timestamp and optimistic protocols keep the database both fast and reliable.

Alright, Kaustubh, let’s dig into *how* the system actually stops those phantom rows from sneaking in. When you run a range query—say, “SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE salary > 5000”—the concurrency‑control protocol doesn’t just lock each individual row it reads; it also places a **predicate lock** on the *condition* itself, essentially saying “no one may insert or delete any tuple that would satisfy salary > 5000 while I’m still working.” In a timestamp‑ordering scheme, each transaction gets a unique start‑time stamp, and before T1 can read the range it checks the **write‑timestamp** of every existing row in that range; if any row has a later write‑timestamp, T1 aborts because a newer transaction has already modified the set. Conversely, when T2 later tries to insert a new employee with a 6000 salary, the system looks at the **read‑timestamp** of the range lock held by T1; because T1’s timestamp is older, T2’s write is considered conflicting and T2 is forced to wait or abort, preserving serializability. If you’re using MVCC, the database will create a new version of the row with a higher commit timestamp, but the query’s snapshot view is anchored to T1’s start timestamp, so that new version is invisible to T1—again no phantom appears. The nuance is that predicate locks can be coarse (locking the whole table) or fine‑grained (locking index intervals), and the choice impacts performance: tighter locks prevent more phantoms but increase contention, while looser locks rely on timestamps and validation to catch conflicts at commit time. So, in practice, you’ll see a combination: the range is locked or its timestamps recorded, the transaction runs, and at the end the system validates that no newer writes have entered the range; if they have, the transaction rolls back and retries, guaranteeing that the result set you saw was a consistent snapshot.

In short, preventing phantoms lets every concurrency‑control scheme give you a consistent view, no matter whether it’s locking, timestamp‑based, or version‑based.
